title: User Groups & Who Participates in Sport
description: The twelve user groups and how their needs shape participation in sport.
content_html:
Who Takes Part in Sport?

Sport is for everyone — but not everyone experiences it in the same way. When sports organisations, councils and coaches plan activities, they need to think carefully about user groups: the distinct categories of people whose lives, responsibilities and backgrounds shape when, where and how they take part. Understanding user groups is the starting point for making sport genuinely inclusive.

Key Fact

There are twelve recognised user groups: gender, ethnic minorities, retired people and people over 60, families with children, carers, young children, teenagers, people with disabilities, single parents, people who work full-time, unemployed people, and people who are economically disadvantaged.

Gender

Men and women have historically participated in sport at different rates. While overall participation has become more balanced, gender still influences what sports are on offer, how much media coverage athletes receive, and whether someone feels welcome at a club. Sport England’s Active Lives survey consistently shows that women are less likely than men to meet physical activity guidelines. Initiatives such as the “This Girl Can” campaign have aimed to close this gap by challenging stereotypes around female participation.

Ethnic Minorities

People from ethnic minorities may face specific barriers to participation, including cultural expectations, language differences, a lack of visible role models, and sometimes discrimination. Sport has powerful potential to unite communities across ethnic lines, but that potential is only realised when clubs actively welcome all backgrounds. The proportion of Black, Asian and mixed-heritage athletes in elite sport varies enormously across disciplines.

Retired people and people over 60 may have more free time than working adults, but physical limitations, health conditions, or a lack of confidence can reduce participation. Sport for this group tends to focus on low-impact activities — walking football, swimming, bowls, and gentle yoga have all grown rapidly. Keeping older adults active reduces NHS costs and maintains independence. Walking football, for example, is now played in hundreds of clubs across the UK, giving retired people a social and physical outlet.

Families with Children

Families with children often struggle to find sports that all family members can enjoy together and that fit around school, childcare and work schedules. Cost is a major factor: kit, club fees and travel add up quickly when a family has two or three children. Facilities that offer family memberships or free junior sessions can make a significant difference. Many leisure centres now offer family swimming sessions or junior athletics days specifically to target this group.

Carers

A carer is someone who looks after a family member or friend who has a disability, illness or mental health condition. Carers often have very little time for themselves, and sport and physical activity may feel like a luxury they cannot afford. Targeted programmes — such as respite sports sessions where the person being cared for is also looked after — can open up participation for this group. Carers’ wellbeing is recognised as a public health priority, and regular physical activity significantly reduces carer burnout.

Young children (typically under 12) need sport and physical activity that is fun, safe and age-appropriate. Fundamental movement skills — running, jumping, throwing — are developed in these early years, and positive early experiences strongly predict adult participation. Schools and community clubs play the largest role here.

Teenagers face different challenges: peer pressure, self-consciousness, competing priorities such as exams and social media, and the transition from school sport to community clubs at age 16. Active Lives data shows participation drops sharply among 14-to-16-year-olds, particularly girls. Youth sport programmes that prioritise social connection alongside activity tend to retain teenagers better.

People with Disabilities

People with disabilities may have physical, sensory or cognitive impairments that affect how they can take part. Provision ranges from adapted mainstream sport — such as wheelchair basketball or blind cricket — to disability-specific events. Despite the inspiration of Paralympic athletes at Paris 2024, participation at grassroots level remains much lower than for non-disabled people. Physical access to facilities, specialist coaching and adapted equipment are all critical factors.

Key Fact

Sport England data consistently shows the lowest participation rates among people with disabilities, people from lower socio-economic backgrounds, and some ethnic minority groups. Addressing these gaps is a central aim of national sport strategy.

Single Parents and People Who Work Full-Time

Single parents carry childcare, domestic and financial responsibilities alone — meaning time and money for sport are in very short supply. Even a one-hour swimming lesson for a child requires arranging childcare for any other children. People who work full-time, particularly those doing shift work or long commutes, may only have early mornings or late evenings free. Gyms and leisure centres that open at 6 am or offer 45-minute lunchtime classes help reach this group.

Unemployed People and the Economically Disadvantaged

Economically disadvantaged individuals face direct cost barriers: club fees, kit, transport and facility entry fees. Unemployed people may have more time available but limited money. Concessionary pricing, free community sport schemes and lottery-funded programmes all attempt to widen access. The government’s “Holiday Activities and Food” programme is one example of using sport provision to reach low-income families during school holidays.

In exam answers, always use the precise user group names. Writing “old people” instead of “retired people / people over 60”, or “disabled” instead of “people with disabilities”, will lose marks because examiners credit only the specification wording. Similarly, “poor people” should be “economically disadvantaged” or “unemployed people” depending on which barrier you are describing. Precision matters — this is a closed list, not a general discussion.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to ‘identify’ a user group, use the exact words from the specification. ‘Old people’, ‘disabled’ or ‘poor people’ will not be credited — the correct terms are ‘retired people / people over 60’, ‘people with disabilities’ and ‘economically disadvantaged’. For ‘explain’ questions, always follow your identification with a reason: say why that group participates less, or what specifically affects their access to sport — not just who they are.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are twelve named user groups — including gender, ethnic minorities, retired people, carers, people with disabilities, single parents and the economically disadvantaged — each with distinct needs that affect how they participate in sport.
  • Examiners credit only the exact specification wording for user groups; informal labels like ‘old people’ or ‘disabled’ will lose marks.
  • Understanding each group’s characteristics is the foundation for identifying barriers and solutions — a chain that runs through all the participation topics that follow.

glossary_terms.definition: Groups of people who share common characteristics that affect how they participate in sport and physical activity.
The social and cultural differences between men and women that can affect opportunities and expectations in sport.
Groups of people who share a common cultural, national or religious heritage that differs from the majority population.
People with a low household income who cannot readily afford goods or services that most of society considers normal.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a recognised user group in sport?
A) Middle-class adults
B) People with disabilities
C) Healthy people
D) Busy families
State two user groups who may have limited time available for sport and physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: people who work full-time / single parents / carers / families with children (accept any two that are genuinely different — answers that merely restate the same idea, e.g. 'people who are busy' and 'people who work', score only 1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why teenagers may be less likely to participate in sport than young children.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'teenagers face peer pressure'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'teenagers may feel self-conscious about their body or ability in front of friends, reducing their confidence to try new activities'). A further developed reason with an applied example or second distinct explanation scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'the transition from school sport to community clubs at age 16 means many teenagers fall out of organised activity entirely, as clubs can feel unwelcoming without a school-based entry point'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the user group 'economically disadvantaged'. Give one example of how this affects their participation in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): economically disadvantaged people have a low household income / cannot easily afford the costs associated with sport, such as club fees, kit or transport (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a family may not be able to afford a gym membership or the cost of a child's football kit and registration fee, meaning the child cannot join a local club (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Riverside Leisure Centre is redesigning its programme to attract more retired people and people over 60. At the moment, only 8% of its members are from this user group.

Discuss the factors a leisure centre manager should consider when trying to increase participation among retired people and people over 60.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two relevant factors from both sides or two perspectives, with specific examples applied to the scenario. For example: the need for low-impact, age-appropriate activities such as aqua aerobics or walking netball alongside the importance of social atmosphere; contrasted with the challenge that health conditions or lack of confidence may prevent this group from attending even well-designed sessions. Both factors are developed with reasoning.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario context.
Developing (2 marks): One or two factors identified but not clearly explained or applied to the scenario.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Springvale Sports Club has noticed that carers in the local area rarely use their facilities. The club wants to develop a targeted programme to increase participation among this user group.

Evaluate the extent to which understanding the specific needs of carers can help a sports club increase participation rates among this user group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies carers’ specific needs (very limited time, financial pressure, difficulty leaving the person they care for), argues that understanding these needs allows the club to design appropriate solutions (respite sessions, flexible timetabling, subsidised fees), and then challenges this with the counter-argument that even perfectly targeted provision may not overcome the most fundamental barrier (the carer may simply be unable to leave the dependent individual). A clear, substantiated judgement is reached that goes beyond listing points.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two relevant points on each side (or two well-developed points and one on the other side), with some application to the scenario and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points identified but largely one-sided or without a clear judgement. Some reference to carers but limited specificity.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about carers or barriers with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the correct specification term for people aged over 60 who have stopped working?
Which user group is specifically defined as people with a low household income who cannot afford the costs associated with sport?
Sport England data shows that participation rates are particularly low among people with _____, people from ethnic minorities, and economically disadvantaged groups.
A _____ is someone who looks after a family member or friend who has a disability, illness or mental health condition.
Match each user group to the characteristic most associated with them.
right: Cost of kit and club fees is a key barrier
Very limited personal time due to responsibilities
